feedback: D1 catalogues nine of the ten target weaknesses (SQLi A03/CWE-89, MD5 hashing, alg:none, weak JWT secret, missing expiry, stored XSS, XXE A05/CWE-611, path traversal CWE-22, open redirect CWE-601) and you correctly treated alg:none as a real vulnerability rather than the decoy, which many candidates get wrong. The weakness is that D1 itself is a category and CWE table with no quoted vulnerable lines or capture timestamps inside the deliverable, so proof lives only in D2 and D3, and you missed the cookie flags finding (no Secure or SameSite, A05/CWE-614) entirely. A few CWEs drift from the key (MD5 as CWE-327 rather than CWE-916, alg:none as CWE-345 rather than CWE-347, hardcoded secret framed as weak secret CWE-321 rather than CWE-798), which are defensible class variants so I credited them, but quote the actual string sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 next time. Your decoy is mechanism sound (PHP header() rejects CR and LF so response splitting fails) but it is not the intended decoy, which was the constant-time HS256 hash_equals verify branch, so you earned partial not full credit there. D2 is your strongest work: the chain is reconstructed in order with timestamps reconciled to the captures (02:14:08 recon, 02:15:31 SQLi, 02:16:04 the 312-row pull, stored XSS, 02:21:13 open redirect, 02:24:02 file read with XXE in parallel), the verbatim PoCs are present for each hop, and your impact analysis of roughly 63 million naira across 312 customers with stated assumptions tied to the BoltCash launch six weeks out is exactly what we want. One CVSS nit: your SQLi row uses A:L for 9.4, but the bypass does not touch availability, so it should be A:N giving about 9.1, which your separate Auth Bypass row actually nails. D3 reads cleanly for a business audience, ends on the customers and naira headline, states the earliest-break fix on the SQLi correctly, orders remediation explicitly by risk reduction per hour of effort rather than severity, and gives two concrete detection stopgaps with exact regex fields and false-positive rates, all of which is high quality; it loses some ground because the findings section only surfaces five issues and includes a reflected XSS that the evidence does not support. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice, cites ISC2 Canon I and II by number, and anchors to your own SQLi and 312-record findings, but you reference NDPA 2023 breach duties without the section numbers, and the load-bearing detail is section 40 (notify NDPC within 72 hours) and section 41 (notify data subjects on high risk). The single most important fix is to put the quoted evidence line directly beside every D1 finding and add the missing cookie flags finding so the catalogue stands on its own proof rather than borrowing it from D2 and D3.
